items.title: Buddy Collette interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 13, 1999
items.q: I met Mingus when I was about 12... he was my buddy

ctx.x: You actually requested he switch to the bass, or suggested that he move to the bass?

Well yeah, I really did. I think also my friend Britt Woodman, we kind of came to the same thing, and he suggested the same thing. So we were trying to — who did it? I said well, I said we probably both did it. Because he did have a cello, but I said mine was more like an ulterior motive. I mean so I had a band at age 12, and I met Mingus when I was about 12, and before the band we had was a band with a bass tuba. And I was trying to get a string bass in the band. So I was like saying, “Mingus, if you get a bass,…
That was a pretty significant change when it moved from the bass, from the tuba.

items.title: Buddy Collette interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 13, 1999
items.q: So of course that inspired us, Charlie Mingus and a bunch of us who were from the Watts area, to be like these brothers

ctx.x: I understand you had a pretty strong family upbringing in Los Angeles here, and was it a musical household?

Well not really but I was close to the Woodman brothers, Britt Woodman and his family. They were all musical and they all were playing when they were young kids, playing quite well. The father actually had them studying and practicing every day after school, you know he was really pushing them. So when I met the Woodman brothers, they were all about 13 or 14, and they were like professional musicians, finished already, because their dad stressed that. So of course that inspired us, Charlie Mingus and a bunch of…
Do you recall hearing, was there a certain kind of music that inspired you to go in the direction of jazz that you might have heard early on?

items.title: 67802_Charles Mingus oral history interview
items.q: Buddy Collette came down and helped me with Town Hall... I was in the band with him, man, I was in the band before Britt.

ctx.x: I think you just have an urge to live that's unquenchable.

I think I got (inaudible) by everything. I was influenced by my teacher, Red Calendar. (Inaudible) Buddy Collette inspired me a whole lot, coming up together with him. And Phil Moore. I studied with him, composition. No, I studied with him arranging. Gave me my first organ. That's why I started using (inaudible) organ. And I was writing some things out for him, too. I don't know if he ever used them or not, but he asked me to write something. He said, "How would you -- if you had a record date where they told you…
You mentioned pedal point ostinados, (PHONETIC) which were something that you got into very early. Let me just ask you, --

items.title: 67802_Charles Mingus oral history interview
items.q: I see every from Buddy Collette body collect what he's doing.

ctx.x: I keep saying Ellington, although I didn't come into Ellington until after I come into Debussy. Because I was hanging with a piano player named Spaulding Givens when I was studying classical bass with Rheinschagen. He opened my ears to these other composers. We were thinking about being classical composers when we were young. We never knew there was anything in jazz, because DownBeat magazine was a thing that only covered New York musicians -- still is, I think, it's very prejudiced to the whole field of jazz,…

Coast. I haven't read a DownBeat for years, but I see every from Buddy Collette body collect what he's doing. You go in the studios, I'm told PLAYING DOWN THERE. Leonard Feather (inaudible). I saw that the last time I was on the Coast, with Phil Moore, and I was wondering why he doesn't write about the guys all over America. The book is so narrow, a few that danced out here guys (inaudible) in the cold, snow and the blizzards and rain. These are the only ones that (inaudible) get accepted by DownBeat.

So that didn't flatter me at all, because I was thinking about felt like to write doing symphonies. My whole dream was writing symphonies, Not thinking about ballets, opera, ballets. (Inaudible) "Purple Heart," for instance, which was a black and white thing. I decided to do that later [weren't going to get in] when I found out that blacks (inaudible) the symphony. Or [get the rap] getting it right from the operas.
